To confirm: targeted genetic testing (EDA gene), focused dental exam/panorex, formal sweat/thermoregulation test, and dermatologic exam for sparse scalp/body hair.

2. Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (Clouston syndrome) — Fits nail dystrophy and progressive hair loss without necessarily having hypohidrosis or dental anomalies; autosomal dominant GJB6 mutations. To confirm: genetic testing for GJB6, dermatologic exam, family history re-check.

3. Alopecia universalis (autoimmune) — Childhood-onset alopecia that can involve eyelashes/eyebrows and sometimes causes nail changes; absence of regrowth since age 2 is compatible with long-standing AA totalis/ universalis. To confirm: dermatology evaluation, scalp/body hair exam, hair pull/trichoscopy, nail exam, autoimmune screen (ANA, thyroid function), consider scalp biopsy if uncertain.

4. Atrichia with papular lesions (HR gene mutation) — Presents with normal or sparse hair at birth with irreversible loss in early childhood; typically genetic and noninflammatory. To confirm: HR gene testing, inspection for keratinous papules, dermatologic/genetic consultation.

5. Trichothiodystrophy or other inherited hair shaft/ectodermal syndromes — Can cause early-onset brittle/sparse hair, nail changes and other systemic signs (photosensitivity, ichthyosis, developmental delay) — less likely here given limited systemic features but considered given nail involvement. To confirm: hair shaft microscopy (polarized light for sulfur-deficient “tiger-tail” banding), genetic testing, review for systemic features.

Recommended immediate next steps (highest yield): targeted history/exam for dentition and sweating, focused dermatologic scalp and body hair exam with trichoscopy, panoramic dental x‑ray, and referral for genetic testing (start with EDA and GJB6 panels).
